DIRECTORS’ DUTIES TO CREDITORS WHEN A CALIFORNIA CORPORATION IS INSOLVENT — THE TRUST FUND DOCTRINE, THE “ZONE OF INSOLVENCY,” AND ASSIGNMENTS FOR THE BENEFIT OF CREDITORS (BERG & BERG ENTERPRISES, LLC V. BOYLE; CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 493.010, 1800, 1802; CORP. CODE §§ 2005, 2300) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jane Doe, states what California law provides about the duties a corporation’s directors owe to the corporation’s creditors when the corporation is insolvent or is heading toward insolvency, and about the statutory procedure — the general assignment for the benefit of creditors — that California law makes available as an alternative to liquidation in bankruptcy. The controlling California decision is Berg & Berg Enterprises, LLC v. Boyle (2009) 178 Cal.App.4th 1020, in which the Court of Appeal held that insolvency alone creates no broad fiduciary duty running from directors to creditors, defined the narrow duty that the trust fund doctrine does impose, and rejected the “zone of insolvency” theory imported from Delaware. The sheet also sets out the statutes that define a general assignment for the benefit of creditors, the assignee’s notice and claims-bar duties, the assignee’s power to recover preferences, and the Corporations Code definition of when a debt has been “adequately provided for” in a winding up. Where a specific business name appears below, that is Acme, Inc.; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what these authorities say. It states the law. It does not evaluate whether any corporation is insolvent, whether any director has breached any duty, whether any transfer is recoverable, or what any court would decide.

WHOSE INTERESTS THE BOARD SERVES — THE RULE BEFORE INSOLVENCY ENTERS THE PICTURE
Berg & Berg Enterprises, LLC v. Boyle begins from the settled proposition that a California corporation’s directors owe their fiduciary duty to the corporation and to its shareholders, a duty the court described as derived from the common law and now also set out by statute in Corporations Code § 309(a). The court then recorded a negative: California has no statute establishing or recognizing that insolvency, or the approach of insolvency, shifts or adds a duty running to the corporation’s creditors. The court also identified the reason the question is hard rather than merely unanswered — in financial distress the interests of shareholders and of the corporation itself may collide with those of creditors, so duties owed to each constituency may conflict and the scope of each becomes difficult to fix. The court cited Pittelman v. Pearce (1992) 6 Cal.App.4th 1436 for the related point that corporate bondholders, unlike shareholders, are owed no fiduciary duty and hold the obligations their contract gives them.

INSOLVENCY BY ITSELF CREATES NO BROAD DUTY TO CREDITORS
The holding of Berg on the central question is stated in the negative. Under the current state of California law, as the Court of Appeal put it, there is no broad, paramount fiduciary duty of due care or loyalty that the directors of an insolvent corporation owe to the corporation’s creditors solely because the corporation is insolvent, whether that duty is said to derive from the Delaware chancery decision in Credit Lyonnais Bank Nederland N.V. v. Pathe Communications Corp. or from any other source. The court declined to create such a duty, giving two reasons: a duty running to creditors would conflict with and dilute the duties directors already owe to shareholders and to the corporation, and a director would face the practical problem of determining objectively and concretely when the state of insolvency that triggers the duty has arrived.

WHAT THE TRUST FUND DOCTRINE DOES REQUIRE — THE SCOPE OF THE DUTY BERG RECOGNIZED
Having refused to recognize a general duty to creditors, Berg defined the narrow duty that California law does impose. The scope of any extracontractual duty owed by directors to an insolvent corporation’s creditors is limited, consistent with the trust fund doctrine, to avoiding actions that divert, dissipate, or unduly risk corporate assets that might otherwise be used to pay creditors’ claims — conduct that, the court added, would include self-dealing and the preferential treatment of creditors. The court then stated the two-part consequence: insolvency alone does not create the duty, and application of the doctrine requires in addition that directors engaged in conduct that diverted, dissipated, or unduly risked corporate assets that might otherwise have gone to satisfy creditors’ claims.

This would include acts that involve self-dealing or the preferential treatment of creditors."
  — Berg & Berg Enterprises, LLC v. Boyle, (2009) 178 Cal.App.4th 1020, 1041 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2260375/berg-berg-enterprises-llc-v-boyle/)

WHERE THE TRUST FUND DOCTRINE COMES FROM AND THE OLDER CALIFORNIA CASES APPLYING IT
The trust fund doctrine is not new law. Berg described the older California authority as applying the doctrine where all of the assets of a corporation, immediately on its becoming insolvent, become a trust fund for the benefit of all of its creditors. The opinion collected the California cases it found applying the doctrine and described what each involved: Saracco Tank & Welding Co. v. Platz (1944) 65 Cal.App.2d 306, statutory liability imposed on directors for the wrongful distribution of all the assets of an insolvent foreign corporation to preferred creditors; Commons v. Schine (1973) 35 Cal.App.3d 141, a controlling partner’s preference in paying an insolvent partnership’s debt to his own creditor corporation; Title Ins. etc. Co. v. California Dev. Co. (1915) 171 Cal. 173, a company controlling an insolvent development corporation’s preferential payment of that corporation’s debts; and Bonney v. Tilley (1895) 109 Cal. 346, directors of an insolvent corporation who were themselves creditors and who secured a preference for their own claims over those of other creditors. The pattern Berg drew from them is that recovery has been allowed where insiders took corporate assets or preferred favored creditors, not merely because the corporation failed.

THE “ZONE” OR “VICINITY” OF INSOLVENCY IS NOT A TRIGGER IN CALIFORNIA
Berg also disposed of the theory that duties to creditors arise before insolvency, when the corporation is said to be operating in the “zone” or “vicinity” of insolvency. The court gave two reasons and then held: every California case applying the trust fund doctrine appears to have involved an entity that was actually insolvent, and the existence of a zone or vicinity of insolvency is even less objectively determinable than actual insolvency. On that basis it held that California law prescribes no fiduciary duty owed to creditors by the directors of a corporation solely by virtue of its operating in that zone or vicinity. The plaintiff in Berg was the corporation’s largest creditor, and its theory was precisely that the duty had arisen while the company was in the zone of insolvency; the judgment dismissing its complaint was affirmed.

A NEGATIVE RESULT THE COURT RECORDED: NO PUBLISHED CALIFORNIA CASE HAD DECIDED THE QUESTION
Berg recorded what it could not find. As of 2009 there were apparently no published California cases that relied on or postdated Credit Lyonnais and decided, by accepting or rejecting its rationale, whether corporate insolvency triggers fiduciary duties of due care and loyalty owed by directors to creditors in this state. The court reached its own conclusion by reasoning from the older trust fund cases and from federal and out-of-state decisions discussing the question, not by following a California decision on point. That absence is part of the holding’s context: Berg is the decision that filled the gap it described.

HOW THE STANDARD WAS APPLIED TO THE FACTS IN BERG
Berg also shows what the duty looks like in operation. Stating the rule affirmatively, the court said that upon actual insolvency directors continue to owe fiduciary duties to shareholders and to the corporation, and owe creditors the duty to avoid diversion, dissipation, or undue risk to assets that might be used to satisfy creditors’ claims. Applied to the pleading before it, that standard was not met. The directors had made an assignment for the benefit of creditors instead of investigating a creditor’s proposed bankruptcy reorganization that would have sought to extract value from the corporation’s accumulated net operating losses. Those facts, the court held, involved neither self-dealing nor prohibited preferential treatment of creditors, and did not constitute the actual diversion, dissipation, or undue risking of the corporation’s assets that were otherwise available to pay creditors’ claims. The court added that directors were not obliged to pursue speculative, contingent and potentially risky alternatives in order to facilitate one creditor’s plan, and that they owed no paramount duty of loyalty to that creditor above other constituencies.

HOW FEDERAL BANKRUPTCY COURTS HAVE READ BERG — AND WHAT THEY SAY REMAINS UNSETTLED
Two federal bankruptcy decisions applying California law show both the reach of Berg and the limits of what it settled. In Solution Trust v. 2100 Grand LLC (In re AWTR Liquidation Inc.) the court quoted Berg’s holding and read it to mean that upon insolvency duties to creditors do not supersede or dilute duties to stockholders; instead creditors join stockholders in being able to sue directors derivatively for breaches of fiduciary duty to the corporation that divert, dissipate, or unduly risk corporate assets. That court said it was not persuaded the California Supreme Court would reach a different conclusion, and stated at the outset that some issues of California law are not settled, so that it had to predict how the California Supreme Court would interpret directors’ and officers’ duties. In Swimmer v. Moeller (In re Moeller) the same holding of Berg was quoted and applied to a claim against a director of an insolvent corporation.

THE ASSIGNEE’S POWER TO RECOVER PREFERENCES — CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE § 1800
Code of Civil Procedure § 1800 gives the assignee under a general assignment a preference-recovery power that parallels the federal one. Berg & Berg Enterprises, LLC v.
